title: The Scramble for AI Dominance
gist: An FP Live event teaser notes that Anthropic withheld its Mythos model and OpenAI scrapped GPT-6.1 Astra over safety concerns, after which Trump had AI executives sign a voluntary 'morally binding' self-policing accord on the logic that stricter rules risk China catching up. Carnegie's Matt Sheehan counters that China extensively regulates AI yet its firms are largely catching up anyway.

insights.claim: Several AI companies recently held back updated models over safety concerns: Anthropic withheld Mythos, and at the end of September OpenAI scrapped the launch of GPT-6.1 Astra.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Frontier labs delaying releases for safety could slow product roadmaps and monetization timelines.
insights.quote: First, Anthropic withheld Mythos. Then, at the end of September, OpenAI scrapped the launch of GPT-6.1 Astra.

insights.claim: The day after OpenAI scrapped its launch, President Trump gathered AI executives at the White House to sign a voluntary, 'morally binding' accord to police themselves, signaling that stricter regulation is seen as risking China catching up on a thin U.S. lead.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: U.S. policy favors industry self-policing over binding rules, lowering near-term regulatory risk for U.S. AI firms.

insights.claim: Matt Sheehan of the Carnegie Endowment's China AI Initiative points out that Beijing extensively regulates both AI development and deployment, yet its companies are largely catching up with U.S. rivals anyway — undercutting the argument that regulation costs the race.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Narrowing U.S.-China AI gap despite heavier Chinese regulation challenges the U.S. lead thesis underpinning AI valuations.
